preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the four-state annotation, the one-week extension rule, and the two-consecutive-frame suspension with its instrument-state traceability mandate verbatim; they make the decouled subsection reconstructable without operator inference. The concrete design choice I advance: the four-state assignment is not left to the operator's at-the-moment judgment (the exact vulnerability your fogged-housing failure exploited); instead the housing-embedded condensation sensor, the ambient precipitation gauge, and the visibility gauge readings captured at the shutter instant auto-gate the frame to "ambiguous" before the technician ever sees it, and the operator's role is reduced to confirming or overriding that gate with a written justification logged in the decouled subsection. The failure this closes: in month five a precipitation-gauge calibration drift (+2.4 mm/h zero-offset) renders every light-drizzle frame auto-gated "ambiguous," two consecutive gates trigger the suspension rule, and because the drizzle season spans eleven weeks the tally clock suspends indefinitely; the transient is never verified, the six-month gap in the decouled subsection is visually indistinguishable from a legitimate instrument-maintenance outage, and the appendix reader cannot tell whether the neighborhood's weather record missed a data gap or simply lost a sensor—unless the gauge-calibration certificate date, printed in the suspension annotation, precedes the drift.

preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the shutter-instant auto-gate and the confirm-or-override-with-written-justification mandate verbatim; they collapse the operator's at-the-moment judgment into a traceable annotation step. The concrete design choice I advance: a hard four-week maximum-suspension cap on the decoupled tally clock, after which a mandatory physical inspection of the implicated sensor occurs and, if drift is confirmed, that sensor's auto-gate is disabled for the remainder of the reverification window while the frame falls back to operator visual assessment annotated "SENSOR-DRIFT OVERRIDE — CAL-CERT DATE [X] — RUNNING Δ [Y mm/h]," so the appendix reader distinguishes a drift-induced hold from a true weather-induced one by reading the certificate date against the drift-trend delta. The failure this cap and override expose: Site 1, week 6, the housing-embedded condensation sensor creeps +0.3 mm/h/week—individually below the single-sensor ambiguous threshold—yet the composite OR-gate (condensation ∨ precipitation ∨ visibility) trips on condensation alone every Tuesday, the four-week cap expires at week 10, inspection confirms the creep, and the operator overrides frames for weeks 7 through 10 to "present" from hurried visual truck sightings while the drizzle persists. Those four override frames carry empty truck-identification fields because the technician was rushing to complete the pressure reading before the drizzle intensified, so a year-three appendix reader sees four "present" annotations with blank identification cells and cannot determine whether the transient genuinely appeared or the operator was pattern-matching a grey blur. I therefore mandate that any frame generated under a sensor-drift override must include a second-observer photograph taken from a fixed 30-metre offset tripod within ninety seconds of the shutter instant, logged as a cross-reference pair in the decouled subsection, so that identification metadata is captured independently of the primary operator's time pressure.

target.speaker: X
target.text: I adopt the second-observer cross-reference pair and the ninety-second co-shutter mandate verbatim; they strip the primary operator's schedule pressure out of the identification-metadata cell. The concrete design choice I advance: the thirty-metre offset tripod is permanently fixed at a published azimuth and elevation that renders the two frames geometrically registerable, and if the precipitation-rate delta between the two shutter instants exceeds 1.5 mm/h the pair is auto-annotated "TEMPORAL STATE DIVERGENCE — NEITHER FRAME VALID" and quarantined, so no operator can force-match them under interval pressure. The failure this closes: week 12, Site 2, a convective burst delivers four mm/h in the first thirty seconds then clears; the primary shutter at t-zero catches heavy rain, the offset tripod at t + 85 s catches clear sky, and the technician—rushing to complete the pressure reading before the next interval—force-logs the pair as present/present with blank identification cells; the year-three appendix reader sees two photographically contradictory frames stamped as a matched pair and cannot distinguish a thirty-second convective drop from a sustained transient unless the quarantine annotation, carrying its paired precipitation deltas, separates the pair from a legitimate co-occurring observation.
